title: Inception ships Mercury 2.5, a diffusion LLM at 1,107 tokens/sec
subtitle: A production-ready diffusion language model claims a 40% intelligence gain over its predecessor at frontier-comparable pricing — the first serious challenge to autoregressive-only orthodoxy.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Inception announced Mercury 2.5 on September 8, 2026 — the company's third-generation diffusion language model. Instead of generating one token at a time, Mercury 2.5 produces and refines multiple tokens in parallel, benchmarked at 1,107 tokens per second on standard GPUs. Inception claims a 40% intelligence gain over Mercury 2, a 260,000-token context window, and 65,536-token maximum output. Pricing is $0.04 per million input tokens and $0.15 per million output tokens, with an 80% launch discount running for a limited window. The model is available on Inception's API, OpenRouter, and Baseten, with tunable reasoning levels, parallel tool calls, and schema-aligned JSON output.

The claim worth watching is the architecture, not the benchmark. Every frontier model shipped by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI, and Meta so far in 2026 has been autoregressive — predicting one token at a time, left to right. Diffusion models, which have dominated image generation since 2022, generate the whole output at once and iteratively refine it. Mercury 2.5 is the first production diffusion LLM at frontier-adjacent quality and price, and the throughput number matters because it is the mechanism by which agentic workloads become economically viable: a tool-calling agent that would take a minute on GPT-6 Astra can complete in seconds if the base model is 5–10x faster per token.

Broader context: 2026 has been a year of architectural experimentation after two years of scale-only progress. Nvidia's Groq-3 LPX and OpenAI's Jalapeño inference chips both target autoregressive throughput; state-space models (Mamba variants) and mixture-of-experts approaches (Alibaba's Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, Moonshot's Kimi K3) have carved out cost-per-token niches. Diffusion LLMs were the sleeper category — Inception and a few academic labs have been publishing since 2024, but nothing shipped at frontier price/performance until now. If Mercury 2.5 holds up under third-party evaluation, expect the big labs to accelerate their own diffusion research; if it does not, expect the category to remain a curiosity.

Takeaway for learners: architectural diversity is coming back after a period where 'transformer + more compute' was the whole answer. If you are early in an ML career, this is a good moment to actually read the diffusion papers — DDPM, score matching, the connection between diffusion and score-based generative modeling — because a working knowledge is about to be worth more than it has been in three years. Reading the Inception blog post is a lot cheaper than waiting for the textbook.
